blocks.text: Read the chapter with this setting in view: Five repeated discourse-ending formulas organize large teaching collections without proving one universally accepted symbolic outline. It gives a starting point for following the chapter's own movement. The chapter itself should determine how far the point is taken. A more precise reconstruction remains disputed.

For a later or comparative connection, note that Matthew, Mark, and Luke receive messenger and Elijah language in relation to John the Baptist, while Romans quotes Jacob-Esau language. This remains a secondary connection rather than the chapter's first-audience context. It can be traced further without replacing the chapter's own setting. Interpretations differ on some details.
